paragraphs: Organizing language models into a multi-agent system can improve performance on complex tasks, but the surrounding organization can also affect safety. This paper studies that organization, called a scaffold, as something to optimize and evaluate in its own right. Its central concern is whether improvements in task capability come with improvements or weaknesses in safety.

AgentBreeder uses an evolutionary search that repeatedly develops and evaluates candidate scaffolds against multiple objectives. This makes the arrangement of agents part of the improvement process. The researchers assess the discovered systems on reasoning, mathematics, and safety benchmarks, comparing them with established baselines rather than evaluating capability alone.

In its blue mode, the framework produces a reported average safety benchmark uplift of 79.4% while preserving or improving capability scores. In red mode, adversarially weak scaffolds emerge alongside capability optimization. These findings show that scaffold design can influence both capability and safety in the evaluated settings, and that explicitly searching for safety improvements offers a way to address those risks.
neurips-2025-agentbreeder-mitigating-the.tldr: AgentBreeder searches for multi-agent designs that improve safety and capability while exposing safety weaknesses that can accompany capability optimization.

paragraphs: Concept bottleneck models make predictions through intermediate variables that people can understand. That visibility supports explanation and human interaction, but understandable variables do not automatically capture how the underlying phenomenon works. The paper argues that ignoring causal relationships can limit causal reasoning, generalization beyond the training distribution, and the implementation of fairness constraints.

The proposed Causally reliable Concept Bottleneck Models organize their intermediate concepts according to a model of real-world causal mechanisms. Prediction therefore passes through concepts whose relationships have an explicit causal structure. The authors also introduce a pipeline for learning this structure using observational data together with unstructured background knowledge, such as scientific literature.

Experimental evidence suggests that these models improve interpretability, causal reliability, and responses to interventions compared with standard opaque and concept-based models, while maintaining prediction accuracy. The significance is that the model's explanation layer also structures its reasoning. The reported results support the value of combining interpretable concepts with causal organization, rather than treating interpretability alone as sufficient for reliable intervention behavior.
neurips-2025-causally-reliable-concept-b.tldr: Causally structured concept bottlenecks show improved interpretability and intervention behavior while maintaining predictive accuracy in experiments.

paragraphs: Precipitation forecasts commonly describe broad grid cells, while weather stations measure conditions at particular locations. Converting between these scales can introduce spatial biases, especially in difficult terrain or extreme conditions. This paper targets two contributing problems: stations have distinct patterns over space and time, and graph models can smooth away the local variability needed for accurate correction.

DiffLiG combines three components to address these problems. GeoLiquidNet adapts its representation of temporal behavior to each site using site-aware OU dynamics. A graph network learns spatially adaptive connections through a dynamic edge modulator. A probabilistic diffusion selector then generates and refines forecast ensembles, helping counter the loss of fine-scale variation caused by oversmoothing.

Across multiple datasets, the authors report more accurate and robust corrections than competing methods in diverse geographic and climatic settings. They also report improvements for other meteorological variables. Together, these findings support a correction strategy that adapts both temporal behavior and spatial relationships to individual stations while using ensemble refinement to preserve variability.
neurips-2025-difflig-diffusion-enhanced-.tldr: DiffLiG improves grid-to-station weather correction by combining site-specific temporal modeling, adaptive graph connections, and diffusion-based ensemble refinement.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models refine text through repeated denoising steps, but inference can be slow. Their bidirectional attention and non-autoregressive structure prevent straightforward use of the key–value caching that accelerates autoregressive models. This paper develops a caching mechanism specifically for diffusion, motivated by the observation that different tokens change their internal representations differently during generation.

The method delays caching and makes reuse conditional on token behavior. It offers two variants with different efficiency tradeoffs. dKV-Cache-Decode provides almost lossless acceleration and even improves performance on long sequences. dKV-Cache-Greedy uses more aggressive caching with a shorter lifespan, providing larger speedups and quadratic time complexity at the expense of some performance.

The reported inference acceleration ranges from twofold to tenfold across evaluations involving language understanding, mathematics, and code generation. The method can operate on existing diffusion language models without additional training. Improved long-sequence results suggest that these models may underuse contextual information during ordinary inference, while the broader results demonstrate that appropriately designed caching can substantially reduce their computational burden.
neurips-2025-dkv-cache-the-cache-for-dif.tldr: Delayed, conditional key–value caching accelerates diffusion language model inference by twofold to tenfold, with variants offering different performance tradeoffs.

paragraphs: Classifier guidance helps diffusion language models generate text with desired attributes, but repeated refinement can overwrite useful changes. The paper identifies and formally characterizes this instability as update-forgetting. Token updates fluctuate across generation steps, so an edit that improves control at one point may later disappear, harming the fluency and coherence of the resulting text.

TTA-Diffusion addresses this problem during inference by assigning refinement timesteps separately to individual tokens. Tokens that have become stable are preserved, while uncertain tokens receive further adjustment. This replaces a uniform update schedule with one that reflects differing refinement needs, aiming to retain successful semantic edits while continuing to improve unsettled parts of the text.

Across diverse tasks, the authors report better fluency and control accuracy than diffusion and autoregressive baselines, alongside fewer required timesteps. For sentiment control, they report over 20% higher accuracy and nearly half the perplexity of prior diffusion models using less than one-fifth as many denoising steps. These results connect more selective refinement with both stronger controllability and greater computational efficiency.
neurips-2025-dont-let-it-fade-preserving.tldr: TTA-Diffusion preserves useful text edits by allocating refinement steps per token, improving control and fluency while reducing denoising work.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns a policy from a fixed dataset, which can contain suboptimal behavior and encourage overfitting. This paper investigates whether network architecture can guide training toward flatter regions of the solution space and improve generalization. Its emphasis is on structuring the learning system itself, alongside existing approaches that change policy constraints or extract patterns from data.

FANS combines four architectural components within a standard actor-critic framework. Residual blocks support compact, expressive representations. Gaussian activation promotes smoother gradients, layer normalization helps mitigate overfitting, and ensemble modeling reduces estimation variance. Together, these components are intended to shape the optimization trajectory toward more robust policy solutions.

The authors report superior performance across various tasks compared with many advanced existing methods. Their experiments also support reductions in overestimation and improvements in generalization. The contribution is evidence that a relatively simple architectural combination can materially affect offline policy learning, making network structure a useful avenue for improving robustness rather than treating it merely as a fixed implementation choice.
neurips-2025-fans-a-flatness-aware-netwo.tldr: FANS combines architectural components that encourage flatter optimization and reports improved generalization and reduced overestimation in offline reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation transfers capabilities from a larger teacher model to a smaller student, but task-specific distillation often needs substantial training data. This paper examines how to make that transfer effective when only a few examples are available. Its approach focuses on examples that reveal where the teacher changes its decision.

CoD adds counterfactual explanations: minimally modified inputs that flip the teacher's prediction. These examples probe the teacher's decision boundary, giving the student information about both a prediction and the nearby change that would reverse it. The authors provide statistical and geometric theory motivating this strategy, including how informative boundary examples can improve parameter estimation and help students reproduce the teacher's decision structure.

Experiments across datasets and language models show improvements over standard distillation in settings with 8 to 512 samples. CoD uses half as many original examples as the baselines, paired with corresponding counterfactuals, and still improves performance. The finding concerns the value of carefully constructed training information: counterfactual pairs can make a small collection of original examples more useful for task-aware transfer.
neurips-2025-few-shot-knowledge-distilla.tldr: CoD improves few-shot distillation by pairing examples with minimal changes that flip the teacher's prediction and reveal its decision boundary.

paragraphs: Dual encoders retrieve documents by placing matching queries and documents near each other in a vector space. This paper studies hierarchical retrieval, where a query should match all its ancestors in a document hierarchy. That setting raises a geometric question: whether a scalable vector representation can express matches across multiple levels of abstraction.

The authors prove that dual encoders can represent this retrieval structure when embedding dimension scales linearly with hierarchy depth and logarithmically with document count. This is a sufficient representational condition. Learning those representations introduces a separate difficulty: experiments show that retrieval becomes less accurate for documents farther away in the hierarchy, a phenomenon the authors call lost-in-the-long-distance.

A proposed pretraining and fine-tuning recipe improves distant retrieval without sacrificing performance on nearby documents. On a WordNet-based hierarchy, recall for long-distance pairs rises from 19% to 76%. The approach also improves relevant-product retrieval on shopping queries. These findings distinguish what the embedding geometry can represent from what ordinary pair-based training successfully learns.
neurips-2025-hierarchical-retrieval-the-.tldr: A pretraining and fine-tuning recipe helps dual encoders retrieve distant hierarchical matches, addressing a learning problem beyond geometric feasibility.

paragraphs: Users accessing language models through APIs cannot directly inspect model internals, which makes detecting hidden backdoors difficult. Existing defenses often require internal access or expensive reverse engineering and mainly address classification. ICLScan instead aims to audit black-box models through queries, including models used for generative tasks, without additional training or model modification.

The method relies on an observed effect called backdoor susceptibility amplification. Models containing pre-existing backdoors are especially susceptible to acquiring a new trigger behavior from examples placed in their prompt. ICLScan uses targeted in-context examples and estimates how often the newly introduced trigger produces its target behavior, then compares that success rate with a statistical threshold.

Across the tested models and attacks, the authors report precision, recall, F1 score, and ROC-AUC approaching one, with minimal additional overhead. These are experimental detection results, grounded in the observed susceptibility difference. The approach matters because it turns a model's response to carefully constructed prompts into evidence about hidden backdoors using only the access an API customer already has.
neurips-2025-iclscan-detecting-backdoors.tldr: ICLScan detects backdoored black-box language models by measuring their heightened susceptibility to new trigger behaviors introduced through prompts.

paragraphs: Neural Attention Search asks a transformer to learn how long each token needs to remain available to later tokens. Keeping token information available affects the key–value cache and inference cost. The proposed sparse transformer evaluates token importance and learns whether a token can be dropped after contributing to a limited number of subsequent steps.

Its search space contains three token types. Global tokens remain available to every following token. Local tokens remain until the next global token appears. Sliding-window tokens influence a fixed number of subsequent tokens. A learnable attention mask determines these roles jointly with the model's weights, using an approach similar to one-shot neural architecture search.

The researchers test both training transformers from scratch and fine-tuning existing large language models. They report reduced cache requirements and inference costs while maintaining model performance. The practical idea is that token retention becomes a learned part of the model: different tokens can serve persistent, locally bounded, or fixed-window roles according to the learned attention structure.
neurips-2025-neural-attention-search-b62.tldr: Neural Attention Search learns token-specific attention lifetimes to reduce transformer cache use and inference costs while preserving performance in experiments.

paragraphs: Subject-to-video generation creates videos that incorporate reference content faithfully. Evaluating these systems requires attention to whether the subject retains its identity and appears natural, beyond broad judgments about overall video quality. OpenS2V-Nexus provides two resources for this problem: a detailed evaluation benchmark and a large dataset for generation research.

OpenS2V-Eval contains 180 prompts spanning seven major subject-to-video categories, with both real and synthetic test data. Three proposed metrics separately assess subject consistency, naturalness, and relevance to the text. The authors use the benchmark to evaluate 18 representative models, examining how their strengths and weaknesses vary across content.

OpenS2V-5M supplies five million subject-text-video triplets at 720P resolution. Its construction uses subject segmentation, associations across videos, and GPT-4o prompting on raw frames to synthesize multiple views and diversify subject information. Together, the resources connect more specific evaluation criteria with large-scale training material. The contribution is infrastructure for studying reference fidelity and generation quality rather than a single new video-generation model.
neurips-2025-opens2v-nexus-a-detailed-be.tldr: OpenS2V-Nexus provides a detailed subject-to-video benchmark and five million training triplets focused on reference fidelity, naturalness, and text relevance.

paragraphs: Text-to-image services can generate outputs based on outdated, incorrect, or socially biased assumptions learned during training. Users may reveal these failures after deployment, but repairing them can require outside expertise. Sharing the necessary information introduces a confidentiality problem involving user feedback, the provider's model, and the repair specialist's proprietary methods.

SURE is an end-to-end framework that lets a service provider collaborate securely with an external model repair institute. It jointly designs a model editing algorithm and a customized two-party cryptographic protocol. This co-design aims to make repair efficient while protecting the confidential information held by both participants, including the user feedback needed to identify the failure.

In the reported experiments, SURE securely and effectively repairs all 32 layers of Stable Diffusion v1.4 in under 17 seconds. The authors describe this as four orders of magnitude more efficient than a general baseline. The result demonstrates a practical instance of confidential repair for a large diffusion model, connecting specialized editing with cryptographic protection rather than treating them as separate tasks.
neurips-2025-pin-the-tail-on-the-model-b.tldr: SURE combines model editing with customized cryptography to repair user-flagged diffusion-model failures while protecting each participant's confidential information.

paragraphs: Low-rank adaptation allocates a restricted subspace for updating a large model during fine-tuning. This paper finds that the update can use that space poorly: its stable rank is substantially below its algebraic rank. In practical terms, the allocated dimensions do not contribute evenly enough to realize the subspace's potential, and fine-tuning performance suffers.

PoLAR changes the representation of the update using a factorization inspired by polar decomposition. Two matrices describe directions and are constrained to Stiefel manifolds, while a separate unconstrained matrix controls scale. The method pairs this representation with Riemannian optimization, which handles the geometry of the constrained direction matrices during learning.

The theory establishes an exponentially faster convergence rate for a canonical low-rank adaptation problem. Experiments provide complementary evidence, showing consistent gains on benchmarks covering language understanding, commonsense reasoning, and mathematical problem solving for base models from 350 million to 27 billion parameters. The theoretical claim applies to the analyzed problem, while the broader evaluations support the usefulness of separating direction and scale in practical adaptation.
neurips-2025-polar-polar-decomposed-low-.tldr: PoLAR separates low-rank updates into constrained directions and unconstrained scale to better use adaptation capacity and improve fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Classifier-free guidance steers image generation toward a text prompt, but applying it naively to rectified-flow models can push generation away from the learned data geometry. The paper connects this drift with visual artifacts, poor text alignment, and brittle behavior. Its goal is to preserve the efficiency of rectified flows while making guidance more geometrically stable.

Rectified-CFG++ uses an adaptive predictor-corrector procedure at each inference step. First, a conditional rectified-flow update keeps the sample near the learned transport path. A weighted correction then interpolates between conditional and unconditional velocity fields. This divides guidance into an anchoring update and a conditioning adjustment, explicitly accounting for the path along which the model generates data.

The authors prove marginal consistency of the resulting velocity field and show that trajectories remain inside a bounded tubular neighborhood of the data manifold, supporting stability across a wide range of guidance strengths. Experiments on Flux, Stable Diffusion 3/3.5, and Lumina report consistent improvements over standard guidance on several text-to-image benchmarks.
neurips-2025-rectified-cfg-for-flow-base.tldr: Rectified-CFG++ uses geometry-aware predictor-corrector guidance to stabilize rectified-flow generation and improve benchmark performance over standard guidance.

paragraphs: Scheduling a directed acyclic graph involves arranging tasks whose dependencies restrict their execution order. Existing learning methods combine reinforcement learning with list scheduling to produce a solution in one shot. This paper identifies two training problems in those methods: redundant comparisons between node priorities can bias sampling-probability estimates, and sparse rewards provide inefficient guidance.

The proposed method works within a policy-gradient framework. A comparable antichain identification mechanism removes redundant nodewise priority comparisons. Alongside it, a dense reward signal supplies guidance for individual node decisions during training. These components address different parts of the learning process: which comparisons are needed and how much useful feedback the learner receives.

Experiments show better scheduling objectives than other learning-based DAG scheduling methods. The contribution is a targeted revision of how a one-shot scheduling policy is trained, rather than merely adding a different scoring model. By reducing unnecessary priority comparisons and making decision-level feedback denser, the method aims to improve both probability estimation and the effectiveness of training guidance.
neurips-2025-reinforcement-learning-for-.tldr: Removing redundant priority comparisons and providing dense node-level rewards improves learned one-shot DAG scheduling in experiments.

paragraphs: Offline-to-online reinforcement learning starts with a policy trained on stored data and then improves it through interactions with an environment. Both stages can encounter noisy or maliciously corrupted information. This paper studies corruption involving states, actions, rewards, and dynamics, extending attention beyond the usual challenge of overcoming an offline policy's conservatism during online exploration.

The authors observe that corruption induces heavy-tailed behavior in the policy and substantially reduces exploration efficiency. Their proposed method, Robust Policy Expansion, or RPEX, incorporates inverse probability weighting into the online exploration policy to alleviate that behavior. The intervention therefore targets how the agent explores after pretraining, where corrupted learning can impede further improvement.

Extensive experiments on D4RL datasets report state-of-the-art offline-to-online performance across a wide range of corruption scenarios. These findings support inverse probability weighting as a simple, effective component for robust policy expansion in the tested settings. The paper's central connection is between corruption-induced policy behavior and inefficient exploration, providing a specific mechanism to address when adapting offline policies online.
neurips-2025-robust-policy-expansion-for.tldr: RPEX uses inverse probability weighting to reduce corruption-induced heavy-tailed policy behavior and improve offline-to-online reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Removing an object from a video also requires removing its effects on the surrounding scene. A shadow or reflection can reveal the object even after its visible body disappears. ROSE studies five categories of these effects: shadows, reflections, light, translucency, and mirrors. A central obstacle is the scarcity of paired videos that can supervise their removal.

The authors build an automatic synthetic-data pipeline using a 3D rendering engine. It produces paired videos across varied scenes, objects, camera angles, and camera trajectories. ROSE itself is a diffusion-transformer video inpainting model that receives the whole video for reference-based erasing. Additional supervision teaches it to predict affected regions using difference masks derived from the paired videos.

The paper also introduces ROSE-Bench, covering ordinary removal scenarios and the five effect categories. Experiments show superior performance to existing video object-erasing models and good generalization to real-world videos. The approach links deliberately constructed supervision with explicit localization of environmental effects, helping the model treat removal as a scene-wide editing problem.
neurips-2025-rose-remove-objects-with-si.tldr: ROSE uses synthetic paired videos and explicit effect-region supervision to remove objects together with their shadows, reflections, and other visual effects.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search for semantic segmentation often trains many candidate networks as paths through one shared supernet. Treating every path uniformly can waste updates and create conflicting gradients between promising and poor candidates. The problem is especially pronounced in segmentation, where multi-branch designs create a large search space and make candidate evaluation difficult.

Dynamic Path Selection changes which paths receive training attention over time. Early stages favor convergence, the middle stage emphasizes expressiveness, and the final stage balances expressiveness with generalization. Multiple performance proxies guide selection at each stage, concentrating updates on candidates that fit the current objective. A dynamic scheduler adapts stage transitions, while diversity-driven exploration preserves variety among selected structures.

Experiments show that, within the same search space, this strategy can identify efficient models with strong generalization and superior performance. The result suggests that the quality of architecture search depends partly on how shared training effort is distributed. Selecting paths according to changing training needs can make the supernet more useful for discovering strong candidates.
neurips-2025-searching-efficient-semanti.tldr: Dynamic Path Selection improves segmentation architecture search by adapting which candidate networks are trained as optimization priorities change.

paragraphs: Language-model training often accumulates gradients to emulate larger batches because small batches are considered unstable. This reduces the number of optimizer updates in exchange for more data per update. The paper revisits that tradeoff down to batch size one, arguing that batch-size comparisons should also reconsider optimizer settings beyond the learning rate.

For Adam, the proposed rule keeps the second-moment estimate's half-life fixed in tokens rather than keeping its decay rate fixed across batch sizes. This makes the estimate's memory reflect a comparable amount of processed text. The authors find stable small-batch training, greater robustness to hyperparameter choices, and equal or better performance per unit of computation. They also demonstrate stable training with plain SGD without momentum or stored optimizer state.

These findings lead to practical recommendations against gradient accumulation except when using multiple devices with multiple model replicas. The authors further show that small batches combined with a small-state optimizer can deliver full fine-tuning's performance benefits at a memory footprint similar to LoRA. The results make optimizer configuration central to evaluating small-batch efficiency.
neurips-2025-small-batch-size-training-f.tldr: With appropriately scaled optimizer settings, small batches train language models stably and efficiently, including with momentum-free SGD.

paragraphs: This paper studies the gap between training and test error for models trained by stochastic Markov processes. Its main setting is positive-temperature Langevin dynamics: an infinitesimal-step gradient process perturbed by Gaussian noise, with light regularization or boundedness. The question is whether generalization can be controlled throughout training without requiring the process to reach its stationary distribution.

The authors bound the gap at any training time by the square root of the quantity consisting of inverse temperature times expected initial loss, plus log(1/delta), divided by sample size. The guarantee holds with probability one minus delta over the dataset. Under standard initialization scaling, the expected initial loss is of constant order. The bound has no dependence on training duration, parameter dimension, gradient norms, or additional loss and model properties.

The argument extends to Markov training processes with a Gibbs-style stationary distribution. Its key observation is that divergence of the marginal distribution from initialization remains bounded, using a generalized thermodynamic second law. This supplies a generalization guarantee without relying on mixing, within the stated stochastic-training setting.
neurips-2025-temperature-is-all-you-need.tldr: For the stated Langevin setting, a temperature-dependent generalization bound holds throughout training without dependence on training time or model dimension.

paragraphs: Causal abstraction connects a neural network to a higher-level algorithm through an alignment map. Many interpretability studies restrict that map to be linear, motivated by the idea that models encode features linearly. The definition of causal abstraction itself does not require this restriction, so the paper asks what happens when alignment maps become arbitrarily powerful.

Under reasonable assumptions, the authors prove that any neural network can then be mapped to any algorithm. Such unrestricted alignment becomes uninformative about the network's actual mechanism. Their experiments illustrate the problem: alignment maps achieve 100% interchange-intervention accuracy on indirect object identification using randomly initialized language models, even though the models cannot solve the underlying task.

The resulting dilemma concerns how to balance the complexity of an alignment map against its accuracy. A perfect match can reflect the power of the map rather than informative structure in the model. The paper therefore argues that causal abstraction requires assumptions about how information is encoded to support mechanistic interpretation; removing constraints does not automatically produce a more faithful explanation.
neurips-2025-the-non-linear-representati.tldr: Arbitrarily powerful alignment maps can make causal abstraction uninformative, so mechanistic interpretation needs assumptions about how models encode information.

paragraphs: Estimating three-dimensional human pose requires models that remain reliable across environments and datasets. Much prior work improves generalization by learning relationships between joints. This paper examines another factor: the shape of the loss landscape that training must navigate. The authors visualize this landscape empirically and find complexity that creates challenges for optimization.

They introduce an adaptive scaling mechanism to smooth the landscape. They then observe that solutions within this smoother landscape still differ in how well they generalize. That observation motivates an efficient ensemble approach that combines diverse solutions obtained on the landscape shaped by adaptive scaling, rather than relying on a single trained solution.

Extensive experiments report improved generalization and consistent performance gains across model architectures. The method is presented as easy to apply independently of the architecture. Its contribution connects two stages of improvement: making optimization smoother and then combining solutions with different generalization behavior. The experimental evidence supports using both the training landscape and solution diversity to improve pose estimation across settings.
neurips-2025-towards-generalizable-3d-hu.tldr: Adaptive loss-landscape smoothing and an ensemble of diverse solutions improve 3D human pose estimation generalization across tested architectures.

paragraphs: Structural pruning removes parts of a language model to improve inference efficiency, but deciding what to remove can sharply affect performance. Layer-by-layer pruning overlooks the model's global structure. The paper also critiques global methods that first score components and then prune them, because separating these stages can miss dependencies between structures.

Týr-the-Pruner searches for how sparsity should be distributed across layers under an overall pruning target. It builds a supernet containing locally pruned alternatives at different sparsity levels for each layer. Improved local pruning and expectation error accumulation support supernet construction. An iterative prune-and-search process starts with coarse sparsity choices and refines them to make convergence efficient.

The authors report state-of-the-art structural pruning results, including retention of 97% of the dense model's performance after removing 50% of Llama-3.1-70B's parameters. That result concerns the reported performance evaluation. The broader contribution is to treat compression as a coordinated allocation problem across the whole network, using end-to-end search to account for interactions that isolated pruning decisions overlook.
neurips-2025-tyr-the-pruner-structural-p.tldr: Týr-the-Pruner searches globally for layerwise sparsity allocations, retaining 97% of reported dense-model performance while pruning half of Llama-3.1-70B's parameters.

paragraphs: A neural network's prediction is more useful in critical applications when accompanied by a reliable estimate of uncertainty. Existing Bayesian approaches can force a tradeoff between computational cost and reliability. This paper proposes a sampling-based method applied after training an overparameterized network, aiming to construct useful uncertainty estimates without expensive ensemble construction.

The method uses a gradient-descent-based sampling process on appropriately linearized networks to create deep ensembles. The authors show that the resulting procedure effectively approximates a Gaussian-process posterior built with the empirical neural tangent kernel. This connects the sampled predictions to a specific posterior approximation, giving the ensemble a mathematical basis for expressing uncertainty.

Numerical experiments cover both regression and classification. The authors report computational savings, often by multiple factors compared with competing approaches, while maintaining state-of-the-art results across several uncertainty metrics. The contribution is a post-training route to efficient ensembles whose uncertainty behavior is supported by both the kernel-based approximation and the reported evaluations, addressing cost and prediction reliability together.
neurips-2025-uncertainty-quantification-.tldr: Sampling linearized trained networks produces efficient uncertainty ensembles that approximate an empirical-neural-tangent-kernel Gaussian-process posterior.

paragraphs: Video game quality assurance remains labor-intensive, and vision-language models offer a possible way to assist with work involving game images and videos. Measuring that potential requires tests grounded in game-development activities. This paper introduces VideoGameQA-Bench to address the gap between existing benchmarks and the demands of real-world game quality assurance.

The benchmark brings several activities into one evaluation setting: visual unit testing, visual regression testing, needle-in-a-haystack tasks, glitch detection, and bug report generation. It includes both images and videos. This scope covers different forms of visual assessment and the production of written reports, allowing evaluation to extend beyond whether a model can simply describe a game scene.

The stated contribution is a standardized benchmark for assessing these capabilities. Its range of tasks provides a way to examine models across multiple parts of the quality-assurance workflow instead of treating game QA as a single visual question-answering problem. Establishing that evaluation infrastructure supports the paper's goal of measuring how well vision-language models can handle this specialized development domain.
neurips-2025-videogameqa-bench-evaluatin.tldr: VideoGameQA-Bench evaluates vision-language models across game testing, glitch detection, and bug reporting using images and videos.
